Flood Insurance Data

Flood vents and flood openings

Where FEMA has given a community final flood elevations, the community must require, for new construction and substantial improvements, that fully enclosed areas below the lowest floor that are usable only for parking, building access or storage (not a basement) and are subject to flooding let floodwater in and out: either a design certified by a registered professional engineer or architect, or at least two openings with a total net area of at least one square inch for every square foot of enclosed area, their bottoms no higher than one foot above grade (44 CFR §60.3(c)(5)).

Elevated single-family primary-home NFIP policies recorded with an enclosure or crawlspace with proper openings
247,720
Elevated single-family primary-home policies with an obstruction code

FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Policies v3 (obstructionType, elevatedBuildingIndicator), as of August 31, 2026. The figures cover single-family primary-home policies that FEMA marks as elevated buildings and gives an obstruction code. 19,081 more have no code and are left out.

What is recorded under elevated buildings on NFIP policies?

FEMA's obstruction code describes what is below the lowest elevated floor. Here are its five most common codes, in FEMA's words, shortened.

FEMA obstruction codeSharePolicies
Non-breakaway walls, crawlspace or finished enclosure, no machinery or equipment below the lowest elevated floor34.2%84,636
Free of obstruction28.1%69,713
Enclosure or crawlspace with proper openings (not used for rating; not applicable in V zones)22.6%56,048
With obstruction (FEMA's code gives no further detail)7.4%18,397
Non-breakaway walls, crawlspace or finished enclosure, with machinery or equipment below the lowest elevated floor5.7%14,054
Every other code2.0%4,872

A code records how the policy was written, not an inspection today. "Not used for rating" is FEMA's own wording for this code.

What FEMA lists as ways that may lower a bill

FEMA's ways that may lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

What this page cannot tell you

Whether a home's openings meet the rule (only an inspection, an engineer's certificate or an Elevation Certificate can say), what a given product costs, or how much any change would lower a premium. No product or company is named or recommended here.

Sources: FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Policies v3 and its field definitions; rules from agents.floodsmart.gov, ecfr.gov, floodsmart.gov. How we check them.
